fatal_errors: The proposal reduces component-level effective density by introducing void space, not the intrinsic density of HfMoTaTiZr; it therefore changes the comparison from alloy properties to structural performance.
Retaining at least 90% of the bulk absolute strength after removing more than 20% of the load-bearing material is asserted without a geometry-normalized strength definition or supporting evidence.
Neither cited study demonstrates HfMoTaTiZr lattice structures, strength retention near 1000 °C, or stability against creep, buckling, oxidation, and LPBF defects.
Archimedes' principle alone is not an appropriate measure of the envelope-based effective density of an open lattice.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses lightweighting and includes a quantitative falsification test, but it does not reconstruct the target intervention of adding 4.2 at.% Cr by vacuum arc melting. It consequently misses the target's approximately 3.8–4 vol.% reticulated Cr2(Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta) Laves phase, lattice contraction, solid-solution hardening, crack-deflection mechanism, and simultaneous increases in yield strength and fracture strain. The proposed LPBF lattice is a creative engineering alternative, but effective density is not equivalent to alloy density, and absolute load capacity generally falls as load-bearing area is removed. E1 concerns dense additively manufactured CoCrFeMnNi and E2 establishes only LPBF feasibility for a different refractory alloy; neither supports the central lattice-performance claim. A stronger experiment would compare mass-normalized and envelope-area-normalized properties, creep and buckling at 1000 °C, oxidation, and fatigue, while measuring lattice density by mass divided by external-envelope volume.
